summary: Niece of the empress Theodora and wife of Justin II, Sophia shared power with her husband from 565, governed with Tiberius II Constantine during Justin's mental collapse in 573–578, and remained a force at court into the reign of Maurice.
overview: Sophia was the most openly political Byzantine empress of the sixth century after her aunt Theodora. When Justin II lost his reason in 573 she bought a truce from Persia and helped choose Tiberius as caesar, then spent the rest of a long life trying to keep the power she had shared.
greatestFeats: Presided over the funeral of Justinian I in 565, for which Corippus says she wove the shroud
Bought a truce from the Persian king Khosrow I on her own authority in 574
Governed with Tiberius while Justin II was incapacitated from 573 to 578
Gave the jewelled Crux Vaticana to Rome with Justin II
keyAchievements: Shown enthroned beside Justin II on the bronze coinage

birth.note: Her parents are not named; her mother was one of Theodora's sisters, Comito or Anastasia.

death.circumstance: Last recorded at Easter 601; she may have died before or after the fall of Maurice in 602, and was buried beside Justin II.

quickFacts.knownFor: Co-ruling with Justin II and governing during his madness

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Sophia was empress of the Eastern Roman Empire from 565 as the wife of Justin II, and she kept the rank of augusta until her death some time after 601. A niece of the empress Theodora, she married a nephew of Justinian I and helped him take the throne on the night the old emperor died. Contemporaries treated her as a partner in power: the court poet Corippus gave her equal place in his account of the accession, and the bronze coinage showed the couple enthroned side by side.

Her greatest power came after Justin II lost his reason in 573, when she ran the government with Tiberius, commander of the palace guard. When Tiberius became emperor in 578 he refused to leave his wife for her and curbed her influence, but she plotted against him, survived into the reign of Maurice, and is last heard of in 601.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Sophia was born around 530. John of Ephesus and Victor of Tunnuna both call her a niece of Theodora, which makes her the daughter of one of Theodora's two sisters, Comito or Anastasia; if her mother was Comito, her father was probably the general Sittas, whom Comito married in 528. She married Justin, son of Justinian's sister Vigilantia, probably while Theodora was still alive, and the match is generally thought to have been the empress's work. They had a son, Justus, who died young, and a daughter, Arabia, who married the general Baduarius.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Sophia's reputation depends on who was writing. Corippus, whose poem In Praise of Justin the Younger celebrated the new reign, plays on her name, which means wisdom, and presents a pious and dignified partner who weaves Justinian's shroud and prays beside her husband. Hostile writers saw ambition and greed. John of Ephesus, a Miaphysite bishop imprisoned in the persecution of Justin's reign, reports her boasting that the empire had come through her and had come back to her, and that Justin had been struck down for failing to value her. Evagrius tells how the couple kicked the severed head of a murdered rival, and Gregory of Tours, writing far away in Gaul, makes her a scheming and avaricious widow.

None of these writers was neutral, and the stories of cruelty come from men with reasons to dislike her. What they share is more reliable: all of them treat Sophia as a decision-maker, and her recorded actions bear that out. She took charge of repaying the debts Justinian had run up with bankers and money-lenders, which Theophanes says won her praise, and her quarrels with Tiberius were over his lavish spending. Paul the Deacon's tale that she mocked the eunuch Narses by offering him a post among the palace weaving women, provoking him to invite the Lombards into Italy, was written two centuries later and is usually treated as legend.

contentSections.title: Empress of Justin II
paragraphs: Justinian I died on the night of 14 November 565 without naming an heir. Justin, who held the palace office of kouropalates, was already in the Great Palace; with the senate's support he was proclaimed and crowned before his cousins could act, and Corippus describes Sophia arranging Justinian's funeral. She took the name Aelia, used by empresses of the fifth century. The strongest rival for the throne, Justin, son of Germanus, was exiled to Alexandria and murdered there in 568, by Sophia's supporters according to John of Biclaro.

The couple acted together in religion and diplomacy. In 569 they sent a relic of the True Cross to Radegund's convent at Poitiers, a gift celebrated by Venantius Fortunatus in the hymn Vexilla regis and in poems that hailed them as a new Constantine and Helena. They also gave Rome the jewelled cross now in the Treasury of Saint Peter's, whose inscription says that Justin gives Rome his help and his consort gives its adornment.

contentSections.title: Governing for a sick emperor
paragraphs: In November 573 the Persian king Khosrow I captured Dara, the empire's chief fortress on the eastern frontier, and Justin II collapsed into what the sources call madness. Gregory of Tours says Sophia took over the government; Evagrius and Menander Protector, closer to events, say she shared it with Tiberius, commander of the Excubitors. In 574 she negotiated with Khosrow on her own authority and bought a one-year truce, reversing Justin's refusal to pay Persia. Theophanes records that she had bars fitted to the palace windows after Justin tried to throw himself out.

With the senate's agreement, Justin proclaimed Tiberius caesar on 7 December 574 and adopted him as his heir. Sophia seems to have hoped to marry Tiberius once Justin died, but he already had a wife, Ino Anastasia, whom Sophia would not admit to the Great Palace; Tiberius lodged his family in the Hormisdas Palace and visited them each evening.

contentSections.title: Augusta under Tiberius and Maurice
paragraphs: Justin II died on 5 October 578 and Tiberius II Constantine became sole emperor. John of Ephesus says Sophia sent the patriarch Eutychius to urge him to divorce Ino and marry her or her daughter Arabia, and that Tiberius refused. Ino was crowned augusta and Sophia, though still an augusta herself, lost control of affairs. Gregory of Tours reports that she then backed a plot to put Justinian, a son of Germanus, on the throne; Tiberius confiscated much of her property and replaced her servants but left her rank untouched.

When Tiberius lay dying in August 582 he is said to have consulted her about the succession, and the general Maurice, betrothed to Tiberius's daughter Constantina, became emperor. Sophia got on better with Constantina than with her mother. At Easter 601 the two augustae gave Maurice a jewelled crown; he hung it above the altar of Hagia Sophia as his own offering, and Theophanes says both women took it as an insult.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: The Easter of 601 is the last time Sophia appears in the sources. She would have been about seventy, and it is not known whether she lived to see Maurice overthrown and killed in 602. The tenth-century Book of Ceremonies records that she was buried beside Justin II in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Sophia made the empress a visible partner in government. Her image on the everyday bronze follis, enthroned beside the emperor with insignia to match his, is often described as the first time an empress was shown on the coinage with equal regalia. Her regency with Tiberius gave a precedent for empresses governing on behalf of incapable emperors, and the cross she and Justin sent to Rome survives in the Treasury of Saint Peter's Basilica.

timeline.title: Birth

timeline.title: Marriage to Justin
timeline.description: She marries Justinian's nephew, probably by Theodora's arrangement.

timeline.title: Accession of Justin II
timeline.description: Justin is proclaimed in the Great Palace on the night Justinian I dies.

timeline.title: Murder of a rival
timeline.description: Justin, son of Germanus, is killed in Alexandria.

timeline.title: Relic for Radegund
timeline.description: The couple send a relic of the True Cross to Radegund at Poitiers.

timeline.title: Fall of Dara
timeline.description: The loss of the eastern fortress is followed by Justin's mental collapse.

timeline.title: Truce with Persia
timeline.description: Sophia buys a one-year truce from Khosrow I.

timeline.title: Tiberius made caesar
timeline.description: The commander of the guard becomes heir and governs with Sophia.

timeline.title: Death of Justin II
timeline.description: Tiberius II Constantine becomes sole emperor and refuses to marry her.

timeline.title: The crown for Maurice
timeline.description: Her last recorded act: Maurice turns her Easter gift into his own offering.
